Traupman 230, 247

inaequālis, inaequāle

Declension on Wiktionary

irregular (of verbs and nouns)

Traupman’s term: verbum inaequāle, an irregular verb (volō, nōlō, fīō), and inaequāliter dēclīnātur, it is declined irregularly (247). The word is classical in the senses “uneven, unequal” (Ovid, Quintilian); Lewis & Short gives no grammatical sense. Varro’s word for irregularity in grammar is anōmalia (LL 9.3, Lewis & Short), set against analogia, regularity.

Examples

  • Quārē inaequālia dīcuntur? — Quia dēclīnātiōnēs extrā rēgulam sunt.

    Why are they called irregular? — Because they are conjugated outside the pattern.Traupman 230

  • inaequāle verbum (ut “volō”)

    an irregular verb (like volō, I want)Traupman 334

  • “Duo” inaequāliter dēclīnātur.

    “Duo” is irregularly declined.Traupman 334

See also verb, defective, rule, grammar, declension.
